The claim of undue delegation of legislative power broadly raises 
the challenge of undue power in the Executive and thus naturally 
involves consideration of the interrelated questions of the availability 
of appropriate restraints through provisions for administrative 
procedure and judicial review. These components of fairness are 
themselves elements of statutory and constitutional rights but it is 
appropriate to discuss them in present context because they bear on 
the issue whether there has been undue delegation to the Executive.
The safeguarding of meaningful judicial review is one of the 
primary functions of the doctrine prohibiting undue delegation of 
legislative powers. * * *
The Government concedes and we agree that the Executive s 
actions under the 1970 Act are not immune from judicial review. * * * 
Within two months of the AMC decision, Congress again extended and 
amended the 1970 legislation. The amendments included a detailed statement 
of national policy, extensive congressional findings to justify wage and price 
controls, and more detailed standards to be followed in administering the Act. 
Among these standards was the exphcit duty to be “generally fair and 
equitable.” The amendments also estabhshed specific administrative 
procedures and, as Judge Leventhal had aheady held, expressly stipulated 
that the rulemaking provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) 
applied to administration of the Act. Congress also provided for judicial review 
of wage and price orders, including appellate review of district court decisions 
by a Temporary Emergency Court of Appeals. See generally Harold Leventhal, 
Principled Fairness and Regulatory Urgency, 25 CASE W. Re s . L. Re v . 66 
(1974).
Judge Leventhal’s predictions for how certain legal constraints would 
operate on the delegated power may have been overly optimistic. His opinion 
emphasizes that actions under the Act would be subject to judicial review. But 
standards against which courts might measure administrative performance 
were absent from the statute itself, and while they might in principle arise 
from regulations promulgated by the agency, or from the pattern of agency
